news_summary: Physicists have made a breakthrough by successfully controlling the magnetic properties of a single atom, advancing quantum technology and atomic-scale manipulation.
news_summary_fr: Les physiciens ont réalisé une avancée majeure en parvenant à contrôler les propriétés magnétiques d'un atome isolé, ce qui fait progresser la technologie quantique et la manipulation à l'échelle atomique.
news_summary_es: Los físicos han logrado un gran avance al controlar con éxito las propiedades magnéticas de un solo átomo, lo que supone un paso adelante en la tecnología cuántica y la manipulación a escala atómica.

articles.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
articles.summary: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.
articles.content:
Researchers at Delft University of Technology (The Netherlands) have accomplished something that physicists previously thought should not be possible. Using radio waves, they managed to directly control the magnetic spin of the nucleus inside a single atom. The unexpected result challenges existing assumptions about how atomic magnetism behaves and could eventually lead to new ways of storing and retrieving quantum information.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, also present scientists with a new puzzle. Although the experiment demonstrated that this remarkable level of control is possible, researchers do not yet fully understand the mechanism that makes it work.

The Hidden Magnetism Inside Every Atom

Atoms in magnetic metals such as iron and nickel behave like tiny magnets. However, the magnetism within an atom comes from different sources. Both electrons and, in some cases, the atomic nucleus possess a quantum property called spin, which can be thought of as a miniature magnetic compass needle.

"By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world."

That protection makes nuclear spin especially interesting to quantum researchers. Because it is less exposed to disturbances from its surroundings, it could offer a promising way to preserve delicate quantum information.

To investigate these tiny magnetic properties, Otte's team uses a specially modified scanning tunneling microscope. This powerful instrument allows the researchers to deliver electrical signals to individual atoms with extraordinary precision.

Until recently, their experiments concentrated primarily on electron spin because it is easier to detect and measure. The nucleus's magnetic spin could only be observed indirectly through a phenomenon known as the hyperfine interaction, which creates a subtle quantum connection between the spins of the electron and nucleus. This connection can cause the two spins to become slightly entangled, meaning their quantum states are linked.

An Atomic Experiment Produces an Unexpected Result

In the latest study, lead author Hester Vennema and her colleagues took a different approach. They simultaneously applied two separate signals to a single atom, with one directed at the electron and the other at the nucleus.

By using these signals together, the researchers could investigate their effects independently. What happened next caught them by surprise.

Even when the electron and nuclear spins were largely disentangled, the team was still able to flip the orientation of the nucleus's magnetic spin. Based on their previous understanding, the nucleus should not have responded in this way.

"According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope."

The result suggests that the interaction between electrical signals and nuclear spin involves a mechanism that scientists have yet to fully explain.

Controlling Quantum Spins Like Guitar Strings

Achieving this level of precision required the researchers to adapt a technique called double magnetic resonance so it could operate on a single atom. The method allowed them to manipulate the magnetic behavior of the atomic nucleus separately from that of an electron.

Magnetic resonance works by applying a wave signal at a carefully selected frequency to change the orientation of a magnetic spin. However, quantum mechanics restricts these changes to specific allowed transitions, meaning the frequency must be precisely matched to the spin being targeted.

Vennema compares the process to playing a musical instrument.

"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The "notes" of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin."

In other words, electrons and atomic nuclei respond to very different frequencies, much as different guitar strings produce different musical notes. By tuning their signals to the appropriate frequencies, the scientists could address the two types of spin separately.

A Quantum Breakthrough With a Mystery Still to Solve

The discovery could have important implications for the future of quantum information technology. Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum systems can use quantum states to encode information in more complex ways.

One major challenge is keeping those states stable long enough for information to be stored and retrieved reliably. Nuclear spins are attractive candidates for quantum memory because they are relatively well isolated from environmental interference.

The ability to control these spins directly could therefore open new possibilities for writing, storing, and reading quantum information. However, the findings represent an early experimental advance rather than a ready-to-use quantum memory technology.

For now, one of the most important outcomes is the new scientific mystery the experiment has revealed. The researchers have demonstrated an unexpected way to manipulate nuclear spin, but the physical mechanism responsible remains unclear.

"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out."

articles.personality_title: Scientists control the magnetic spin of a single atom's nucleus for the first time
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Atoms act like tiny magnets because of a property called spin, found in both electrons and sometimes in the nucleus. While electron spins are strong and easier to study, nuclear spins are weaker but better protected from outside disturbances, making them interesting for storing quantum information.

**What happened** – Researchers at Delft University in the Netherlands used radio waves and a scanning tunneling microscope to control the magnetic spin inside the nucleus of a single atom. This direct control was unexpected because scientists thought nuclear spins couldn’t be influenced this way. The team applied two signals simultaneously—one for the electron and one for the nucleus—and managed to flip the nucleus’s spin even when it was mostly separated from the electron.

**Impact** – This discovery challenges previous ideas about how atoms behave and could help build better quantum memory devices. Quantum memory stores information in ways that normal computers can’t, but it’s hard to keep this information stable. Because nuclear spins are well shielded, controlling them directly might make quantum memory more reliable in the future.

**What's next step** – Scientists now need to understand why the nuclear spin responded to the signals, as the mechanism behind this is still a mystery. Further research will focus on figuring out how this control works and how to use it to improve quantum technology.

**One-sentence takeaway** – For the first time, scientists have directly controlled the magnetic spin of a single atom’s nucleus, opening new paths for quantum memory research while uncovering a surprising scientific puzzle.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques contrôlent pour la première fois le spin magnétique du noyau d’un atome
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les atomes se comportent comme de petits aimants grâce à une propriété appelée spin, présente chez les électrons et parfois dans le noyau. Les spins des électrons sont forts et plus faciles à étudier, tandis que les spins nucléaires sont plus faibles mais mieux protégés des perturbations extérieures, ce qui les rend intéressants pour stocker l’information quantique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de l’Université de Delft aux Pays-Bas ont utilisé des ondes radio et un microscope à effet tunnel pour contrôler le spin magnétique à l’intérieur du noyau d’un seul atome. Ce contrôle direct était inattendu car on pensait que les spins nucléaires ne pouvaient pas être influencés de cette façon. L’équipe a appliqué deux signaux en même temps – un pour l’électron et un pour le noyau – et a réussi à inverser le spin du noyau même quand il était presque séparé de l’électron.

**Impact** – Cette découverte remet en cause les idées précédentes sur le comportement des atomes et pourrait aider à construire de meilleures mémoires quantiques. La mémoire quantique stocke l’information d’une façon que les ordinateurs normaux ne peuvent pas, mais il est difficile de garder cette information stable. Comme les spins nucléaires sont bien protégés, les contrôler directement pourrait rendre la mémoire quantique plus fiable à l’avenir.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques doivent maintenant comprendre pourquoi le spin nucléaire a réagi aux signaux, car le mécanisme derrière cela reste un mystère. Les recherches futures viseront à expliquer ce contrôle et à l’utiliser pour améliorer la technologie quantique.

**Une phrase clé** – Pour la première fois, des scientifiques ont contrôlé directement le spin magnétique du noyau d’un atome, ouvrant de nouvelles voies pour la recherche sur la mémoire quantique tout en découvrant un mystère scientifique surprenant.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos controlan por primera vez el giro magnético del núcleo de un átomo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los átomos actúan como pequeños imanes por una propiedad llamada giro, que tienen los electrones y a veces el núcleo. Los giros de los electrones son fuertes y fáciles de estudiar, mientras que los giros nucleares son más débiles pero están mejor protegidos de interferencias externas, lo que los hace interesantes para guardar información cuántica.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de Delft en los Países Bajos usaron ondas de radio y un microscopio de efecto túnel para controlar el giro magnético dentro del núcleo de un solo átomo. Este control directo fue inesperado porque se pensaba que los giros nucleares no podían ser afectados de esa manera. El equipo aplicó dos señales al mismo tiempo—una para el electrón y otra para el núcleo—y logró cambiar el giro del núcleo aunque estuviera casi separado del electrón.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento desafía ideas anteriores sobre cómo se comportan los átomos y podría ayudar a crear memorias cuánticas mejores. La memoria cuántica guarda información de formas que las computadoras normales no pueden, pero es difícil mantenerla estable. Como los giros nucleares están bien protegidos, controlarlos directamente podría hacer que la memoria cuántica sea más confiable en el futuro.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos necesitan entender por qué el giro nuclear respondió a las señales, ya que el mecanismo detrás de esto sigue siendo un misterio. Las investigaciones futuras se enfocarán en explicar este control y usarlo para mejorar la tecnología cuántica.

**Una frase clave** – Por primera vez, científicos han controlado directamente el giro magnético del núcleo de un átomo, abriendo nuevos caminos para la investigación de la memoria cuántica y revelando un sorprendente misterio científico.
